title: Ritzy LA neighborhood descends into bizarre shouting match over old people’s home plans: ‘He’s just a perv’
text:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.

See more of our coverage in your search results.

A heated Los Angeles planning meeting descended into a chaos on Thursday as residents clashed with a developer over housing for the elderly.

Furious Woodland Hills residents battled it out at the public forum with Akhilesh Jah over plans to transform a single-family home into a sprawling senior living facility, according to Fox 11.

At one point, Jah was forced to shout over the crowd: “It’s my turn to speak! When you spoke I didn’t interrupt, did I?”

But the angry audience wasn’t having it.

“He’s just a perv,” one person yelled from the crowd, according to footage from the chaotic Los Angeles City Planning Commission hearing.

“You lie, shame on you!” another woman shouted before officers escorted her from the meeting.

Then things took an even stranger turn.

“I’m going to do black magic on you,” a third person threatened.

The extraordinary scenes unfolded as residents fought against Jah’s proposal to demolish a four-bedroom, three-bathroom home on Del Moreno Drive and replace it with a 71-unit senior living facility featuring a cafeteria and medical office.

Neighbors say the project is wildly out of place in their quiet residential community, and they’re particularly furious that the development would have no parking.

The property sits directly across from Taft High School, with homes on one side and commercial buildings near Ventura Boulevard on the other.

Residents also raised concerns about the location being within an LA Fire Department fire zone.

Jah, an aerospace engineer-turned-developer, said the project would include eight units designated as low-income housing. Under California’s increasingly developer-friendly housing laws, projects that include affordable housing can qualify for incentives allowing them to sidestep certain local restrictions involving density, height and parking.

That has left some residents feeling as though their neighborhood rules have been rendered practically meaningless.

Most of the variances Jah sought were approved by the commission, although the developer still faces additional hearings and permitting. Jah has indicated the project could be years away from construction.

Residents, meanwhile, say they have no intention of backing down.

The bitter Woodland Hills fight is part of a larger battle playing out across California, in which developers are increasingly using state housing laws and density bonuses to propose projects that would have been difficult or impossible to build under traditional local zoning rules, according to the Los Angeles Times.

Jah has spent years studying California housing laws and local zoning regulations, according to the outlet, targeting properties where state incentives could allow substantially denser development.

His projects have sparked fierce opposition in the San Fernando Valley, where residents fear large developments could permanently alter the suburban character of their communities.
